title: Split BST
statement:
`root` is a binary search tree with distinct values, and `target` is an integer that may or may not appear in it. Split the tree into two binary search trees: the first holds every node whose value is **less than or equal to** `target`, the second every node whose value is **greater than** `target`.

Keep as much of the original shape as possible: in each new tree, a node's parent must be its nearest ancestor in the original tree that landed in the same new tree. So a node keeps its old parent whenever that parent goes to the same side, and the node of each side that has no such ancestor becomes that side's root. You may rewire the original nodes.

Return `[small, large]`, the roots of the first and second trees, using `null` for a side that receives no nodes.
constraints: root is a valid binary search tree with distinct values
notes:
## Intuition

Look only at the root. If `root.val <= target`, the root and its whole left subtree belong to the small side, untouched. Only the right subtree is mixed, and splitting it is the same problem on a smaller tree. Its small part holds values above `root.val`, so it becomes the root's new right child; its large part is the whole large answer. The case `root.val > target` is the mirror image. A brute force can follow the rule literally: for every node, walk up to the nearest ancestor on the same side and attach a copy there.

## Approach

1. An empty tree splits into `[null, null]`.
2. If `root.val <= target`: split `root.right` into `small` and `large`, set `root.right = small`, and return `[root, large]`.
3. Otherwise: split `root.left` into `small` and `large`, set `root.left = large`, and return `[small, root]`.

Only the nodes on the search path for `target` are rewired; every other link stays as it was.

## Example 1, step by step

With `target = 2`, the root `4` is large, so split its left subtree `2 -> (1, 3)`. There `2` is small, so split its right subtree `3`. Node `3` is large; its left subtree is empty and gives `[null, null]`, so `3.left` stays `null` and the call returns `[null, 3]`. Back at `2`: `2.right = null`, returning `[2, 3]`. Back at `4`: `4.left = 3`, returning `[2, 4]`. The small tree is `[2,1]` and the large tree is `[4,3,6,null,null,5,7]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(h), where h is the tree height: one call per node on the search path.
- Space: O(h) for the recursion stack.

## Pitfalls

- Nodes equal to `target` go to the **small** side, so test `root.val <= target`.
- `target` may be missing from the tree; the recursion still works because it only compares values.
- When the root goes small, its new right child is the **small** part of the right subtree, and vice versa. Swapping them breaks the search-tree order.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `root` | root of the subtree being split |
| `small` | root of the part with values `<= target` |
| `large` | root of the part with values `> target` |

narration.2: An empty subtree has nothing to split.
narration.3: Both sides of an empty tree are empty.
narration.5: The root belongs to the small side, along with its entire left subtree.
narration.6: Only the right subtree can hold both kinds of values, so split it the same way.
narration.7: Its small part has values above root.val, so it becomes the new right child.
narration.8: The root heads the small tree; the right subtree's large part is the whole large tree.
narration.10: Otherwise the root is large, along with its right subtree; split the left subtree.
narration.11: The left subtree's large part has values below root.val, so it hangs on the left.
narration.12: The left subtree's small part is the whole small tree, and the root heads the large tree.
